scope: Specificity and overstatement corrections to exhibition headings and invitations. Existing image-reviewed memberships, chapter order and artwork roles remain intact.
basis: Saved ensemble-image draft and separate review, direct assistant sheet inspections recorded in assistant-spot-checks.json. These are AI editorial readings, not making-history or intention claims.

nifty-faces--locked-geometry.title: Faces Built from Boxes
nifty-faces--locked-geometry.question: How do rectangular eye sockets and mouth shapes organize a face?
nifty-faces--locked-geometry.introduction: Rectangular frames divide these faces into eye zones, brow bands and mouths. Follow those divisions through flat color areas and increasingly layered lines, then compare works whose compartments are less easy to separate. The rectangles remain useful landmarks even when curved and diagonal marks cross them. Which shapes make recognition possible?
nifty-faces--locked-geometry.closing: Return to an eye socket or mouth in an earlier work. Does its rectangular frame make the feature clearer, or draw attention to the marks crossing it?

nifty-faces--radiating-pressure.title: Lines Beyond the Face
nifty-faces--radiating-pressure.question: What changes when lines extend beyond the outline of a head?
nifty-faces--radiating-pressure.introduction: Start with heads whose boundaries remain easy to follow, then look at the marks extending into the surrounding space. Diagonals, loops and crossing lines connect the features to a larger pattern. Later works make that separation less clear. Follow one line outward and notice when it stops describing a face.
nifty-faces--radiating-pressure.closing: Choose a line that crosses a head's edge. Does it link the face to its surroundings, or make the edge more difficult to follow?

nifty-faces--mismatched-eyes.title: Eyes That Do Not Match
nifty-faces--mismatched-eyes.question: How do differences between eye shapes change where you look first?
nifty-faces--mismatched-eyes.introduction: Compare the two sides of a face before naming its expression. Eye zones can differ in height, size, outline or the marks inside them. This gallery follows those differences into more divided and layered heads, including departures from a simple paired structure. The surrounding mouth and contours offer further points of comparison.
nifty-faces--mismatched-eyes.closing: After looking at each eye separately, look at the whole head again. Which surrounding shapes reinforce the difference, and which help bring the features together?

nifty-faces--silhouette-and-shadow.title: Dark Marks and Bright Areas
nifty-faces--silhouette-and-shadow.question: Which bright and dark areas make a face easier to locate?
nifty-faces--silhouette-and-shadow.introduction: Compare bright contours, colored eyes and pale surfaces with the darker areas around them. Some heads stand against dark surroundings; others place deep eye hollows or layered marks within a lighter ground. Follow those contrasts through sparse and more densely crossed drawings. A small accent can become a useful landmark without fixing the whole face into one reading.
nifty-faces--silhouette-and-shadow.closing: Return to a face that was initially hard to read. Which contrast between light and dark now helps you find its features?

nifty-faces--bared-teeth.title: Teeth and Mouths
nifty-faces--bared-teeth.question: How do tooth shapes and surrounding marks change the reading of a mouth?
nifty-faces--bared-teeth.introduction: Teeth recur across these heads, but their shapes, spacing and surroundings differ. Compare mouths framed by clear contours with those crossed by colored lines or partly lost in shadow. A similar tooth row can sit within quite different facial structures. Keep possible expressions open while looking at what the drawing actually shows.
nifty-faces--bared-teeth.closing: Compare two mouths that first seemed alike. What changes when you attend to individual teeth, the space between them and the outlines around the opening?

nifty-faces--objects-letters-emblems.title: Faces and Signs
nifty-faces--objects-letters-emblems.question: What changes when a facial feature also reads as a letter or symbol?
nifty-faces--objects-letters-emblems.introduction: Crosses, frames, lettering and object-like shapes share space with recognizable facial features. Follow works where a mark has a clear place within a head into images where signs and patterned divisions attract attention of their own. Compare a shape's role in describing a face with its appearance as a separate graphic mark.
nifty-faces--objects-letters-emblems.closing: Choose a sign within one image. Does the face remain recognizable when you look past it, or does that mark supply an essential part of its structure?

nifty-faces--accumulation-and-dissolutio.title: Faces Made of Layers
nifty-faces--accumulation-and-dissolutio.question: How do overlapping color and line keep a face visible?
nifty-faces--accumulation-and-dissolutio.introduction: These heads offer several ways to follow features through overlapping marks. Begin with contours and colored areas that remain readily distinguishable, then compare denser crossings and less certain boundaries. Look separately at the eye, mouth and surrounding surface. Their relationships can become clearer as you alternate between individual marks and the whole image.
nifty-faces--accumulation-and-dissolutio.closing: Find a feature that you briefly lost among the surrounding marks. Which line or color area lets you locate it again?

rawblocks--pressure-and-containment.title: Outline and Interior
rawblocks--pressure-and-containment.question: How do outlines and interior marks take turns directing your attention?
rawblocks--pressure-and-containment.introduction: Follow heads described by open contours into layered faces, geometric divisions and ringed forms. Outlines can separate features, connect them or become a subject of their own. An abstract arrangement of rectangles and bands offers a contrast to the heads around it. Compare what lies inside a boundary with the marks crossing that boundary.
rawblocks--pressure-and-containment.closing: Compare a facial outline with a geometric division elsewhere in the gallery. What does each boundary make easier to distinguish, and what crosses it?

rawblocks--body-in-the-field.title: Figures and Their Surroundings
rawblocks--body-in-the-field.question: How do posture, neighboring bodies and setting change the way you see a figure?
rawblocks--body-in-the-field.introduction: Move between standing and seated figures, heads with radiating marks, groups and bodies described by loose lines. Changes in scale and spacing draw attention toward the surrounding color and setting. Landscape-like passages offer another way to look at those relationships. Compare a body's outline with the shapes continuing beyond it.
rawblocks--body-in-the-field.closing: Look back at an earlier figure after spending time with the final surroundings. Which parts of its setting now attract more of your attention?

rawblocks--face-as-frequency.title: Color, Line and Facial Features
rawblocks--face-as-frequency.question: Which feature draws your attention when colors and lines compete across a head?
rawblocks--face-as-frequency.introduction: Some works make one eye or mouth easy to locate; others divide attention among colored patches, repeated lines and several facial features. Follow those changes through contrasting mouths, eye shapes and layered heads. Notice what you see first, then look for a second point of entry into the same image.
rawblocks--face-as-frequency.closing: Does the feature that first caught your eye still organize the image after longer looking? Try beginning with a different color or line.

nnxyz-other--the-face-as-field.title: Heads Across Different Surfaces
nnxyz-other--the-face-as-field.question: How do outlines and colored areas keep a head recognizable?
nnxyz-other--the-face-as-field.introduction: Follow heads across different combinations of contour, color and overlapping line. Some features remain clearly separated; others share space with patterned marks or additional figures. Compare the outline of a head with the divisions inside it. This gallery offers several ways to recognize a face without assuming that the same shapes do the work each time.
nnxyz-other--the-face-as-field.closing: Choose two heads with different surfaces. Which few features establish each one, and how do the surrounding marks change the way you follow them?

nnxyz-other--figures-in-motion-and-compa.title: Bodies, Signs and Scenes
nnxyz-other--figures-in-motion-and-compa.question: When do surroundings become as prominent as the figures within them?
nnxyz-other--figures-in-motion-and-compa.introduction: A solitary body leads into figures sharing space with signs, other bodies and increasingly prominent surroundings. Compare gesture with the marks that continue beyond a figure. Changes in scale, grouping and setting offer different ways into these scenes. The later works invite attention to light, water and open landscape as well as recognizable characters.
nnxyz-other--figures-in-motion-and-compa.closing: Look back from the final scene to an earlier body. At which point did you begin following the surrounding space as closely as the figure?

scrimshaw--face-as-field.title: Scrimshaw: Faces, Figures and Letters
scrimshaw--face-as-field.question: What connects the overlapping lines in a portrait, a group of figures and lettering?
scrimshaw--face-as-field.introduction: Follow facial contours through increasingly layered heads, then compare doubled forms, grouped figures and lettering. Colored lines can describe an eye or mouth while also forming a pattern across the surface. The final standing figures and the letters in GM offer a concrete comparison with earlier portraits, while keeping their different subjects clear.
scrimshaw--face-as-field.closing: Compare the edges of the letters in GM with a contour in an earlier portrait. How do overlapping lines describe these two different subjects?

nnotb--open-fields.title: A Figure in Open Space
nnotb--open-fields.question: What changes when a figure has room around it?
nnotb--open-fields.introduction: Look at the space around a form before concentrating on its features. This short gallery moves from a landscape-like image and a softly layered head toward small silhouettes, larger figures and dark surroundings. Compare the amount of open ground with the scale of each subject. The relationship can change even when a character remains easy to recognize.
nnotb--open-fields.closing: Return to one of the smaller silhouettes after looking at a larger figure. What does the extra surrounding space make you notice?

nnotb--black-silhouettes.title: Characters in Silhouette
nnotb--black-silhouettes.question: How much can a solid shape tell us?
nnotb--black-silhouettes.introduction: A dark shape can establish a character with only a few additional marks. Follow silhouettes across colored grounds, then compare eye shapes, mouth signs and lines around or within the body. Later works make the dark area less continuous. Notice which details alter recognition while the larger shape remains a useful landmark.
nnotb--black-silhouettes.closing: Compare two silhouettes with different facial marks. What remains recognizable if you look at the larger dark shapes first?

nnotb--gesture-and-stance.title: The Body Makes a Gesture
nnotb--gesture-and-stance.question: Where does movement begin in a still drawing?
nnotb--gesture-and-stance.introduction: Compare the directions of a body, its limbs and the lines around it. Raised arms, bent heads, broad clothing-like forms and quieter upright stances offer different ways to read a pose. Follow changes between sparse contours and layered bodies. A movement suggested by the outline may differ from the direction of the surrounding marks.
nnotb--gesture-and-stance.closing: Choose a pose and follow one line beyond its body. Does that line reinforce the stance, or lead your eye in another direction?

nnotb--figures-in-company.title: Figures in Company
nnotb--figures-in-company.question: When do separate figures begin to form a group?
nnotb--figures-in-company.introduction: Look first at the spaces between figures, then at the marks they share. Pairs and groups can remain separate, overlap or become difficult to distinguish from a common pattern. Follow changes in scale, placement and contour through these drawings. Compare a group whose members are readily distinguishable with one whose outlines cross.
nnotb--figures-in-company.closing: Look back at an earlier pair after the more closely grouped figures. Which gaps, overlaps or repeated shapes make the relationship easier to see?

nnotb--crowded-crossings.title: Finding Faces in a Crowd
nnotb--crowded-crossings.question: What lets one face emerge from a crowded drawing?
nnotb--crowded-crossings.introduction: Begin with recognizable faces surrounded by crossing marks, then follow drawings containing additional heads and figures. A pale outline, a colored area or a gap between lines can become a point of entry. Compare the marks within one head with the crossings between several characters. Dense surfaces do not all organize recognition in the same way.
nnotb--crowded-crossings.closing: Choose a face that took time to locate. Which mark helped you find it, and does the same mark connect it to another figure?

nnotb--creatures-and-objects.title: Characters Beyond the Human Face
nnotb--creatures-and-objects.question: What makes a shape read as a character?
nnotb--creatures-and-objects.introduction: Animal-like silhouettes, unusual bodies and less clearly defined forms offer different paths toward recognizing a character. Look at eye shapes, mouth marks and stance before settling on a name. Some contours support a familiar reading; others leave it uncertain. Compare the details that establish a character with the marks that make its boundaries harder to follow.
nnotb--creatures-and-objects.closing: Return to a form whose identity remains uncertain. Can you describe the visible shapes that suggest a character without deciding exactly what it is?

nnotb--settings-and-light.title: Figures, Places and Light
nnotb--settings-and-light.question: When does the surrounding space become part of the subject?
nnotb--settings-and-light.introduction: Follow surroundings that attract attention alongside a figure: colored grounds, rays, shadow-like areas and landscape-like passages. Some drawings leave room around a recognizable subject; others cross its boundary with the same marks found in the setting. Compare the direction and scale of those marks before deciding which part of the image to follow.
nnotb--settings-and-light.closing: Look at an earlier setting after the final works. Which surrounding shapes now seem as useful for reading the image as the figure itself?

nnotb--letters-and-signs.title: Letters Among the Marks
nnotb--letters-and-signs.question: How does a readable sign change the way we look?
nnotb--letters-and-signs.introduction: Words and signs can give the eye a readable landmark among other marks. Follow lettering within or beside figures, then compare signs that also work as graphic shapes. Framing, placement and surrounding lines can change their prominence. Look for the moment when you begin reading a mark, and when you return to following its outline.
nnotb--letters-and-signs.closing: Choose a readable sign and look at its shape alone. What connects its lines or framing to the surrounding drawing?

nnotb--radiating-lines.title: Lines Moving Outward
nnotb--radiating-lines.question: How do marks carry a figure into its surroundings?
nnotb--radiating-lines.introduction: Follow rays, waves, spikes and loose lines as they spread beyond a central form. Compare a sparse arrangement with repeated marks that occupy more of the surrounding space. The centers change from silhouettes to more layered heads, while the directions of the lines offer another route through each drawing. Notice where your eye travels outward.
nnotb--radiating-lines.closing: Return to a central form after following its surrounding lines. Which direction makes its boundary clearer, and which draws you away from it?

nnotb--bands-and-patterns.title: Across the Surface
nnotb--bands-and-patterns.question: What do bands and repeated marks hold together?
nnotb--bands-and-patterns.introduction: Bands, zigzags, grids and repeated units divide these surfaces in different ways. Follow patterns within a head, along an edge and across a larger field. Some divisions help locate facial features; other arrangements give attention to geometry itself. Compare the repetition of a mark with the changes introduced by color, spacing or an interruption.
nnotb--bands-and-patterns.closing: Choose one repeated unit and follow it across an image. Where does a change in its shape, spacing or color redirect your attention?

nnotb--coils-and-circles.title: Looking into Circles
nnotb--coils-and-circles.question: When is a circle an eye, and when is it a pattern?
nnotb--coils-and-circles.introduction: Circles and coiled lines can describe eyes, repeat as patterns or organize an abstract arrangement. Follow those different roles across rounded sockets, layered heads and less clearly facial compositions. Compare the marks inside a ring with the lines extending beyond it. A similar shape can offer quite different points of entry into these images.
nnotb--coils-and-circles.closing: Compare a circle that reads as an eye with one in an abstract arrangement. Which surrounding marks change the role of the circle?

nnotb--uneven-faces.title: Two Sides of a Face
nnotb--uneven-faces.question: How does a face hold together when its two sides differ?
nnotb--uneven-faces.introduction: Look at the two sides of a head separately before returning to the whole. Differences in eye shape, height, color and surrounding marks can be slight or pronounced. Follow those variations across less divided faces and more contrasting halves. Mouths, contours and repeated lines supply further ways to compare how the features relate.
nnotb--uneven-faces.closing: After comparing both sides, choose a feature that links them. Does it reduce the difference or make it more apparent?

nnotb--mouths-and-teeth.title: The Shape of a Mouth
nnotb--mouths-and-teeth.question: How do similar teeth leave an expression unresolved?
nnotb--mouths-and-teeth.introduction: Compare the shape of a mouth with its teeth, surrounding lines and colored ground. Individual teeth may remain distinct or join a larger band of marks. Follow changes in spacing, framing and jaw shape across different heads. A possible grin or grimace remains a reading to test against the rest of the drawing.
nnotb--mouths-and-teeth.closing: Find two mouths with similar teeth. Which surrounding features change the way you read their expressions?

nnotb--heads-in-darkness.title: Heads Emerging from Darkness
nnotb--heads-in-darkness.question: Which marks let a face become visible against a dark ground?
nnotb--heads-in-darkness.introduction: Look for the marks that make a head distinguishable from dark surroundings. Contours, colored bands, crossed shapes and teeth offer different points of entry. Follow them across more layered or less clearly bounded surfaces. Compare what first draws your attention with the quieter shapes you locate after spending more time with the image.
nnotb--heads-in-darkness.closing: Return to a darker work and begin with a small accent. Which features become easier to find when you follow that mark?

nnotb--blocks-and-volume.title: Building the Head
nnotb--blocks-and-volume.question: What gives a drawn head its structure?
nnotb--blocks-and-volume.introduction: Rectangular divisions, broad color areas and curved contours offer different ways to structure a head. Compare clearly separated facial zones with layered surfaces and more rounded forms. Follow a boundary between two features, then notice the marks crossing it. The apparent shape of a head and its surface pattern can suggest different directions for looking.
nnotb--blocks-and-volume.closing: Choose a head with clearly divided features and compare it with a rounded form. Which lines or color areas establish their different structures?
